/tools.title: Pick a question. Leave with a clearer next move.
/tools.summary: Use a free tool to check a claim, set safer AI rules, untangle a workflow, or decide what kind of system your team actually needs.
/tools.audience: Anyone trying to use AI, evidence, or changing rules without guessing.
editorialIntro: These public tools are useful on their own. They also let you inspect how Aloha AI turns a hard question into visible steps, checks, limits, and a next action.

toolsExperience.intro: You do not need to know which service you need. Start with the question that sounds most like yours.
toolsExperience.privacy: The work happens in your browser. Nothing you enter is sent to Aloha AI unless a tool clearly asks you to submit it.

items.title: Does this source really support the sentence?
items.plain: Compare a claim with its source and find gaps before somebody else does.

items.title: Could this marketing claim need proof or legal review?
items.plain: Screen health, wellness, cannabis, psychedelic, and other regulated-product language.

items.title: How strong is the evidence behind this health claim?
items.plain: Identify the kind of evidence a claim needs and where uncertainty still matters.

items.title: What would this bill actually require?
items.plain: Turn pasted legal text into a map of duties, people, dates, enforcement, and open questions.

items.title: How does the U.S. controlled-substances system fit together?
items.plain: Separate federal scheduling, state law, research rules, medical programs, and changing status.

items.title: How ready is your team to govern AI?
items.plain: Check your written rules, approved tools, privacy controls, verification, supervision, and accountability.

items.title: What belongs in your first AI policy?
items.plain: Create a reviewable starting template for tools, privacy, checking, supervision, retention, and ownership.

items.title: What does governed AI look like while work is happening?
items.plain: Explore a demonstration of sources, checks, permissions, evaluation, and human approval working together.

items.title: Is your AI workflow dependable—or just a habit?
items.plain: Check sources, verification, data handling, repeatability, ownership, and measurement.

items.title: Should this repeated prompt become a real workflow?
items.plain: Turn a useful prompt into steps, sources, checks, outputs, ownership, and failure handling.

items.title: Your team uses AI. What should happen next?
items.plain: Score decision clarity, evidence, governance, workflow, data, and implementation readiness.

items.title: What kind of knowledge system do you actually need?
items.plain: Choose the smallest useful setup based on documents, updates, permissions, evidence, and workflow.

items.title: Could your expertise become a real AI practice?
items.plain: Check domain strength, delivery systems, demand, capacity, AI operations, and intellectual property.

editorialSections.title: A working demonstration you can run yourself

blocks.text: Each public beta turns one difficult question into a small experience you can use now. A custom version may add private data, organization-specific rules, integrations, review gates, and audit records. The public tool demonstrates the approach; it is not evidence that every possible private version has already been commissioned or deployed.
Score your governance, legal AI workflow, or practice against published guidance, and get a prioritized list of what to fix first.
Each tool makes its question, steps, output, and limits visible. A commissioned version is scoped to the organization and may use different sources, controls, and infrastructure.
A weak result is a map. It shows the workflow worth gating, the policy worth writing, or the budget worth scoping before you commit.

editorialSections.title: Pick the one that matches your question

blocks.text: The shelf above is grouped by the question a visitor is trying to answer. Every card still resolves to its canonical record, so status, evidence, methods, and limitations stay synchronized as the platform changes.

Verification and workflow risk for legal teams: citation checking, legal AI workflow diagnostics, regulatory bill analysis, regulated claims review, controlled-substances explanation, and health-claims evidence literacy.
Documented-practice maturity and exposure: governance readiness, policy generation, and culture-governance auditing mapped to the authority the organization actually answers to.
Where your organization stands with AI: assess organizational readiness, practice readiness, workflow maturity, and whether a repeated prompt should become a governed workflow.

Scope the build before you commit: estimate a defensible budget and determine whether your documents need folders, Notion, Airtable, retrieval-augmented generation, a custom application, or simply better standard operating procedures.

editorialSections.eyebrow: These are demonstrations of what I build
editorialSections.title: The version I build for your organization

blocks.text: What you run here is the public, in-browser version. A firm-deployed build routes checks through a private backend, keeps credentials off the client, writes a signed audit record, and integrates with the tools your team already runs. Each tool maps to a real engagement: a citation gate, a documented governance policy, or a scoped budget.

items: Run a tool. Score your readiness or risk in a few minutes; the weak result identifies the workflow, policy, or budget worth addressing first.
Book a scoping call. Talk through what the result means for your organization and what a governed build would cover.
Get it built. Most engagements start with a Systems Audit, the fastest proof of which workflow is worth building properly first.
